title: service-slat-queue-depth-inventory
summary: Exploratory inventory of how queue depth and slab (request group) dynamics map to end-to-end SLAT quantiles. Includes sampling method, per-stage micro-breakdown, cohorts by seq_len/cache-hit/coldstart, hypotheses for high p99s, and prioritized mitigations.
body:
Context and motivation:

We observed intermittent p99 spikes on the Hosted API for medium-length payloads (seq_len 256–1024). This note collects trace sampling, an explicit inventory of request "slabs" (small groups of concurrent requests that interact via batching and queueing), and per-stage cost attribution to see whether queue depth/backpressure or kernel execution variability is the dominant contributor. Goal: actionable mitigations that reduce p99 without regressing throughput/cost.

Sampling and data:
- Time window: 2025-11-01 to 2025-11-07 (7 days), peak traffic hours 09:00–18:00 PT.
- Source: 50k sampled end-to-end traces from the production tracing pipeline (trace_id sample keyed by route).
- Sampling bias: we stratified by route, seq_len (<=64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024), and cache-hit (KV cache hit vs miss).
- Trace fields used: request_enqueue_ts, batch_wait_start, batch_wait_end, gpu_enqueue_ts, kernel_start_ts, kernel_end_ts, kv_lookup_start/end, postprocess_start/end, egress_ts, host_queue_depth (sampled at enqueue time).

Definitions used in this note:
- SLAT (service latency): total egress_ts - request_enqueue_ts.
- Slab: group of requests that contend in the same batching window and whose relative ordering can cause head-of-line effects. We compute slab_id by tracing the batch window id + shard node id.
- Queue depth: number of requests queued on node at the time of enqueue (sample).

Global quantiles (all routes, weighted by requests):
- p50 = 37 ms
- p95 = 172 ms
- p99 = 842 ms
- p999 = 1.9 s

Cohort breakdown (examples):
1) Seq_len <= 64, KV-hit:
- p50 = 22 ms, p95 = 60 ms, p99 = 120 ms
- Per-stage median share: tokenization 5%, batch_wait 10%, kernel_exec 55%, postprocess+egress 30%
2) Seq_len 257–1024, KV-miss, cold-start (worker freshly started last 5m):
- p50 = 160 ms, p95 = 620 ms, p99 = 1.8 s
- Per-stage median share: tokenization 3%, batch_wait 35%, kv_lookup 10%, kernel_exec 35%, postprocess+egress 17%
3) Seq_len 65–256, KV-miss, hot worker:
- p50 = 48 ms, p95 = 220 ms, p99 = 640 ms
- Per-stage median share: tokenization 4%, batch_wait 26%, kernel_exec 42%, postprocess 28%

Key empirical patterns discovered:
- Queue depth correlates strongly with p95/p99 regressions for the 65–1024 seq_len cohorts. Requests sampled with host_queue_depth >= 8 had p95 ~4–6x higher than queue_depth <=2.
- Head-of-line blocking: in slabs where an unusually long kernel_exec (outlier kernel) was present, following requests in the same slab saw inflated batch_wait times (they were held until the long-running request finished or the batch window emitted a small batch).
- Kernel-execution variance alone explains ~40% of p99 mass for >1024 seq_len (huge model compute variance), but for 65–1024 seq_len only ~25% of p99 mass; the remainder is explainable by queueing + batch_wait amplification.
- KV cache misses increase end-to-end SLAT but are not the primary p99 driver except when combined with queue_depth > 4 (miss triggers extra DB hop while requests pile up).
- Cold restarts (worker JIT/initialization) create clear p999 outliers; their frequency is low but skew p999 heavily. These are identifiable in traces by init markers.

Micro-breakdown example (median numbers for affected slab):
- enqueue -> batch_wait_start: 1 ms
- batch_wait duration (median): 48 ms, but in p99 slabs: 410 ms
- kv_lookup (miss): 28 ms
- gpu_enqueue -> kernel_exec: 6 ms (scheduling overhead)
- kernel_exec median: 120 ms, p99 kernel_exec: 680 ms
- postprocess+egress: 18 ms

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Adaptive batching windows are too permissive under high queue depth; large slab sizes amplify single outlier kernel runs into p99s for many requests.
2) We lack prioritization between short and long requests; short requests can be stuck behind long-running kernel executions in the same slab.
3) Backend KV lookup latency tail combined with queue growth introduces bufferbloat: requests wait in batchers while a few requests are slugging DB/redis.
4) Worker cold/slow JIT paths still surface and can cause slab-wide long tails for that worker until warm-up completes.

Evidence linking hypotheses to data:
- Slabs with variance(kernel_exec) in top 5% had an average slab-level p95 3.9x higher than slabs in bottom 50% variance.
- When we filter traces to host_queue_depth <= 2, p99 drops ~45% for the 65–256 cohort.
- Traces with a marked KV-hit have 2.5x lower batch_wait variance than KV-miss slabs at same queue depth.

Short-term mitigations (low-risk, quick):
- Reduce max_batch_wait_ms for routes serving 65–1024 by 30% as an experiment (ENG-4123). Expected: reduce slab amplification at cost of slightly smaller batches and marginal cost increase. Owner: Jared.
- Add a short-lived prioritization token for requests predicted to be short (seq_len <= 128) that lets them bypass a single pending batch if queue_depth > threshold. Quick AB test. Owner: Priya.
- Add explicit measurement tag for worker-warm flag in traces so we can filter cold-run outliers more easily. Owner: Marcus.

Medium-term mitigations (2–6 weeks):
- Implement per-slab probabilistic preemption: if a batch contains an inflight request that is >X ms into kernel_exec, emit the batch early for waiting requests (implement in async-batcher). Risk: more partial/smaller batches. Owner: runtime scheduling team.
- Introduce a small fast-path kernel configuration tuned for short sequences (better for 1–4 token steps at low batch sizes). Owner: infra-kernels.
- Add adaptive KV lookup local cache/pepper layer to reduce tail for common keys; measure effect on batch_wait variance.

Longer-term (quarter):
- Scheduler rewrite to maintain two lanes (low-latency lane and throughput lane) with capacity reservations. This addresses prioritization without sacrificing full throughput.
- Smarter slab formation: incorporate request-token-prediction to avoid grouping long-form requests with many short ones.

Open questions and experiments to run next (with short commands):
- Q1: How does lowering max_batch_wait affect cost per token? Metric: tokens/$ over 3-day AB test.
- Q2: Can we detect impending long-kernel runs quickly (early signs in kernel exec microtraces) and split the batch proactively?
- Q3: Is there an inexpensive heuristic using early microtime slices (first 10ms of kernel exec) to predict long kernels?

Immediate action items (owner, ETA):
- Jared: roll max_batch_wait ms experiment to 10% of traffic for 65–1024 routes (ETA: 2025-12-05) — Jira ENG-4123.
- Priya: design the low-latency bypass AB (spec + metric dashboard) by 2025-11-21.
- Marcus: instrument worker-warm flag and KV-miss marker in traces (PR #1286) by 2025-11-28.
- Ana: run cost analysis baseline for small-batch scenario and report impact on tokens/$ (ETA: 2025-12-08).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory and intentionally mixes descriptive numbers and hypotheses; please comment if you want separate export tables for each route (I can add CSV extracts).
- Be careful reading global p99s: a few worker cold events inflate p999 but are not representative of steady-state SLOs. We should maintain both p99 and p99.9 in dashboards.

Appendix (quick reproducibility):
- Query for sampled traces: select traces where trace.sample_flag = 'slab-sampled' and timestamp between '2025-11-01' and '2025-11-07'; join trace spans on slab_id and compute per-slab variance(kernel_exec).
- Visualizations I used: slab-level heatmap (queue_depth vs slab_variance) and a waterfall overlay per-slab showing per-request batch_wait and kernel_exec timelines. I can add the JSON config for the viz on request.

End.
